As described in Section 2.3.2, this SCM assumes a sophisticated fleet management system, including accurate (perfect in this case) forecasts of vehicle drop-off time, drop-off SOC, and dwell time, as well as the ability to accurately forecast the facility load and PV generation. The EVSE assignment is performed based on whether the vehicle’s energy requirements can be provided within its dwell time using a 25-kW EVSE, or whether a 350-kW EVSE is required. Then, a mathematical optimization problem is solved to calculate EVSE and the battery dispatch set points that result in the least customer impact while maintaining power consumption below the grid ceiling. These precalculated set points are referenced by the SCM in real time. While resulting in a slightly higher peak load—though not likely requiring any distribution infrastructure upgrades—this strategy significantly outperformed the Gold SCM with no DER. Using the Platinum SCM with no DER resulted in 13% of sessions compromised, with an average SOC deficit of 19%. This is compared to 31% and 21% average, respectively, from the Gold SCM with no DER. The addition of DER slightly improved on the previous scenario (Platinum SCM with no DER) with the percentage of compromised sessions dropping from 13% to 8%, but still presenting an average 19% SOC deficit. Comparing this configuration to the Gold SCM with DER in Section 4.1.3, which resulted in a higher 10% of sessions compromised but with a smaller 13% in SOC deficit, we can conclude both configurations performed well while maintaining the overall peak around 2 MW, avoiding the need for any infrastructure upgrades. However, the advantage of the Platinum SCM came from achieving comparable performance while requiring a notably smaller BESS design: 0.5 MW/1 h versus the 1 MW/4 h of the Gold SCM.
